summary: Defines the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF), a data format that incident response teams use to share information about computer security incidents. It gives an information model and an XML Schema data model. It was replaced by RFC 7970.

eli5.summary: Security teams need a common form to fill in when they report a break-in to each other. IODEF is that form, so everybody understands the report. It was replaced by RFC 7970.

questions: how do csirts share incident data
how do security teams share incident data
what is the iodef restriction attribute
subtitle: A common XML format for security teams to describe computer security incidents to each other.

tldr.problem: Computer security incident response teams need help from other parties to stop malicious activity, but they swap incident details as free-form text that analysts must parse by hand.
tldr.mechanism: IODEF defines an information model and an XML Schema for incident data: hosts, networks, services, attack methods, evidence, impact, contacts and the actions the sender wants.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5070 was obsoleted by RFC 7970 and updated by RFC 6685, so it is no longer the current IODEF specification.

today: RFC 5070 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 7970 and updated by RFC 6685. Use RFC 7970 for the current IODEF specification.

sections.title: Why a Shared Incident Format
sections.content:
Organizations often need help from others to deal with malicious activity: working with an ISP to filter attack traffic, asking a remote site to take down a bot-network, or sharing watch-lists of known malicious IP addresses in a consortium. The Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) represents the information that CSIRTs (Computer Security Incident Response Teams) commonly exchange. It is an XML representation for passing incident information across administrative domains.

The data model covers hosts, networks and the services running on them; attack methodology and forensic evidence; the impact of the activity; and limited ways to document workflow. A structured format allows more automation, less effort normalizing data from different sources, and a common basis for interoperable tools.

The RFC is explicit about its limits. It is a transport format, not a good format for on-disk storage or long-term archiving. It does not define what an incident is, only a framework flexible enough for most operators. And procedural, trust and legal obstacles to sharing are not addressed. The text of section 3 and the schema in section 8 are normative; the UML diagrams are not.
sections.eli5: If every school reported lost property in a different way, nobody could match things up. A single lost-property form means everyone can read each other's reports.

sections.title: The Document and Incident Classes
sections.content:
Every IODEF document is an IODEF-Document, which holds one or more Incident elements. The document's version attribute MUST be 1.00, and a lang attribute giving the language is required.

An Incident carries a tracking number (IncidentID), a ReportTime, one or more Assessment and Contact elements, and optional parts such as DetectTime, StartTime, EndTime, Description, Method, EventData, History and AdditionalData. AlternativeID lists the numbers other CSIRTs use for the same incident, and RelatedActivity points to related incidents or URLs.

The required purpose attribute says why the document was sent: traceback, mitigation, reporting, other, or ext-value for extensions. The restriction attribute states how the sender wants the information disclosed: public, need-to-know, private (the default on Incident) or default. It is inherited by child classes, which can override it.

The IncidentID must be globally unique when combined with its name attribute, which MUST be the fully qualified domain name of the CSIRT that created the document.
sections.eli5: The form has a front page with a case number and why you are writing, then boxes for who, when, what happened and who to call. A stamp on it says how widely it may be shared.

sections.title: Impact, Events and Requested Actions
sections.content:
The Assessment class describes the technical and non-technical consequences of an incident. At least one of Impact, TimeImpact or MonetaryImpact MUST be present. Impact classifies the activity with a type such as dos, recon, info-leak or social-engineering, plus an optional severity of low, medium or high and a completion of failed or succeeded. TimeImpact expresses labor, elapsed time or downtime in units from seconds to years.

EventData describes individual events within an incident: the systems involved, techniques, impact and evidence such as logs. While Incident summarizes the whole, EventData is specific, and if the two conflict, the more specific EventData MUST win. EventData can nest, and nested instances inherit values from their parent, so common data like a shared contact is written once. Only leaf instances represent actual events.

The Expectation class tells the recipient what the sender wants done, using an action value such as investigate, block-host, rate-limit-network or contact-source-site. It can also carry a start time, an end time by which the action should no longer be performed, a severity, and the expected actor.
sections.eli5: The report says how bad it was, lists each thing that happened, and ends with what you want the other team to do, like "please block this address".

sections.title: Data Types and Processing Rules
sections.content:
The model uses typed fields, mapped to XML Schema types where possible: base-10 integers and reals, strings, multilingual strings, base64 and hexadecimal bytes, enumerations, date-times in the RFC 3339 subset of ISO 8601, timezone offsets, port lists such as 2,5-15,30,32,40-50,55-60, and postal addresses, names, phone numbers, emails and URLs that follow other standards.

Every IODEF document MUST begin with an XML declaration giving the XML version, and MUST name its character encoding if it is not UTF-8. The characters &, <, >, double quote and apostrophe MUST be escaped. The namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iodef-1.0.

Documents MUST be well-formed XML and SHOULD be validated against the schema. Schema validity alone is not enough, because some rules in the text of section 3 cannot be expressed in the schema. For example, at least one of the aggregated classes in Contact and EventData must be present, and the language values need checking against RFC 4646.

For internationalization, each document MUST declare its language, free-text classes can carry a different language, and free text can be repeated in several languages so one document serves recipients who speak different ones.
sections.eli5: The form has strict rules for how to write dates, numbers and names, so a reader in another country reads them the same way.

sections.title: Extending the Format
sections.content:
New data can be added without changing the schema. To add a new value to an enumerated attribute, set the attribute to ext-value and put the new value in the matching ext- attribute. An extension attribute MUST NOT be set unless the original attribute is ext-value.

New data elements go in the AdditionalData or RecordItem classes. Atomic values set the content and a dtype attribute. XML extensions set dtype to xml, MUST declare their own namespace, and are recommended to use the prefix iodef-. A parser that meets an extension it does not understand MUST ignore it and process the rest. Implementations SHOULD NOT download schemas at runtime for security reasons.
sections.eli5: If the form has no box for what you need to say, there is a blank page at the back marked "other", and readers skip any page they do not understand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The data model itself does not introduce security issues, but incident data may be privacy sensitive to the parties exchanging it or those described in it. Care is needed during exchange and when documents are stored and processed.

The transport used for IODEF MUST provide appropriate confidentiality, integrity and authenticity, and a standardized security protocol is encouraged. A document may request action, so a parser must authenticate the sender and assign appropriate confidence to the data before acting on it.

The restriction attribute only expresses the sender's wishes. The recipient is free to ignore it, and enforcement is not a technical problem.
sections.eli5: A report about a break-in is secret. Lock the envelope, check who sent it, and remember that a note saying "do not share" only works if people respect it.

items.label: Contact source
items.desc: Contact the site(s) identified as the source of the activity.

items.label: Contact target
items.desc: Contact the site(s) identified as the target of the activity.

items.label: Contact sender
items.desc: Contact the originator of the document.

items.label: Investigate
items.desc: Investigate the system(s) listed in the event.

items.label: Block host
items.desc: Block traffic from the machine(s) listed as sources.

items.label: Block network
items.desc: Block traffic from the network(s) listed as sources.

items.label: Block port
items.desc: Block the port listed as sources in the event.

items.label: Rate-limit host
items.desc: Rate-limit traffic from the machine(s) listed as sources.

items.label: Rate-limit network
items.desc: Rate-limit traffic from the network(s) listed as sources.

items.label: Rate-limit port
items.desc: Rate-limit the port(s) listed as sources.

items.label: Remediate
items.desc: Remediate in a way other than rate limiting or blocking.

items.label: Triage status
items.desc: Conveys receipts and the triaging of an incident.

items.label: New information
items.desc: Conveys that new information was received for this incident.

items.label: Other
items.desc: Perform a custom action described in the Description class.

items.label: Extension
items.desc: Escape value used to extend this attribute.
